title: Removing the Nth Node From the End of a List

phrases.explanation: To visit each node in the linked list one by one from head to tail
A special or extreme input scenario that may cause unexpected behavior
An approach that solves the problem by going through the data only once
To keep a fixed distance between two pointers as they move through a structure
A placeholder node placed before the head to simplify edge case handling

technical_terms.definition: A linear data structure where each node points to the next node and the last node points to null
A strategy using two references that move through a data structure at different speeds or with a fixed gap
The first node in a linked list, used as the entry point for traversal
A dummy node added before the head to handle boundary conditions more cleanly
Deleting a node by updating pointers without allocating extra data structures

java_methods.description: A field referencing the next node in the linked list
Creates a new list node with value zero, often used as a dummy node
Appends an element to the end of an array list
Returns the element at the specified index in the array list

concept: Given the head of a singly linked list and an integer n, remove the nth node from the end of the list and return the head of the modified list.

solutions.label: Two-Pass Count and Remove
solutions.summary: First pass counts the total length. Second pass finds and removes the target node.

solutions.label: Store Nodes in Array
solutions.summary: Store all nodes in an array list for direct index access, then remove the target node.

solutions.label: Two-Pointer One Pass
solutions.summary: Use two pointers separated by a gap of n. When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer is right before the target node.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    style N1 fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style N2 fill:#f87171,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. You're given the head of a singly linked list and an integer n. You need to remove the nth node from the end of the list and return the head. For example, given the list one, two, three, four, five and n equals two, you should remove node four and return one, two, three, five.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So we count from the end, not the beginning. A couple of questions: can n ever be larger than the length of the list? And what should I do if removing the node means removing the head itself?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good questions. You can assume n is always valid, meaning it will be between one and the length of the list. And yes, the head itself might be the node to remove. In that case just return the next node.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. Can the list be empty?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: The list will have at least one node.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Alright. So to summarize: given a non-empty singly linked list and a valid n, I remove the nth node from the end and return the updated head. Let me start with a straightforward approach.

sections.title: Two-Pass Count and Remove
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Pass1["First Pass: Count Length = 5"]
        direction LR
        A1[1] --> A2[2] --> A3[3] --> A4[4] --> A5[5]
    end
    subgraph Pass2["Second Pass: Remove node at position 4"]
        direction LR
        B1[1] --> B2[2] --> B3[3] --> B5[5]
    end
    Pass1 --> Pass2
    style A1 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style A2 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style A3 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style A4 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style A5 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B1 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B2 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B3 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B5 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first idea is a two-pass approach. In the first pass I traverse the entire list to count the total number of nodes. If the length is L and I want to remove the nth from the end, that's the node at position L minus n from the beginning.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For our example, the list has five nodes and n is two. So the target is at position five minus two, which is three, meaning it's the fourth node. In the second pass I walk to the node just before it and update its next pointer to skip over the target.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I'll use a dummy node before the head to handle the case where the head itself needs to be removed. The time complexity is O of n since we traverse twice, and space is O of one.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That works. It's clean and correct. Can you think of a different approach, maybe one that trades space for a different style of access?

    end
    subgraph Remove["Access index 5 - 2 = 3 directly"]

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Another idea is to store each node reference in an array list as I traverse. Then I can directly access any node by index. To remove the nth from the end, I access the node at index length minus n minus one, which is the node right before the target, and update its next pointer.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For our example, the array has five entries. I want the second from the end, so I look at index five minus two minus one, which is index two. That's node three. I set its next to node five, skipping node four.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: This is still O of n time but uses O of n extra space for the array. It's a single pass through the list but not ideal on memory.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Right. Can you combine the benefits of both? One pass and constant space?

sections.title: Two-Pointer One Pass
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Step1["Step 1: Advance fast pointer n=2 steps"]
        direction LR
        D0[dummy] --> E1[1] --> E2[2] --> E3[3] --> E4[4] --> E5[5]
    end
    subgraph Step2["Step 2: Move both until fast reaches end"]
        direction LR
        F0["dummy/slow start"] -.-> F3["3/slow end"]
        G2["2/fast start"] -.-> G5["5/fast end"]
    end
    subgraph Step3["Step 3: slow.next = slow.next.next"]
        direction LR
        H1[1] --> H2[2] --> H3[3] --> H5[5] --> HNULL[null]
    end
    Step1 --> Step2 --> Step3
    style E1 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style E2 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style E3 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style E4 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style E5 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style H1 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style H2 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style H3 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style H5 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The optimal approach uses two pointers with a gap of n between them. I create a dummy node pointing to the head. I place both fast and slow at the dummy, then advance fast by n plus one steps so the gap between them is exactly n plus one.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Then I move both pointers one step at a time until fast reaches null. At that point, slow is right before the target node. I simply set slow dot next to slow dot next dot next to remove it.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Walking through our example: fast advances three steps to node two. Then both move together. When fast hits null, slow is at node three. We skip node four by linking three directly to five.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: This gives us O of n time and O of one space with just a single pass. The dummy node cleanly handles the edge case of removing the head.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Excellent. That's the most elegant solution. Let's wrap up with a summary.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Comparison["Approach Comparison"]
        direction TB
        L1["Two-Pass: O of n time, O of 1 space, 2 passes"]
        L2["Array Store: O of n time, O of n space, 1 pass"]
        L3["Two-Pointer: O of n time, O of 1 space, 1 pass"]
    end
    style L1 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style L2 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style L3 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great job. We explored three approaches. The two-pass method is intuitive but requires traversing the list twice. Storing nodes in an array gives random access but costs extra memory. The two-pointer technique achieves the best of both worlds: one pass with constant space.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight is that maintaining a fixed gap between two pointers lets us find the nth node from the end without knowing the total length. The dummy node is a useful trick for simplifying head removal. Thank you!
